idiom_name: fixed thread pool with a leader slot over a shared handle set (join / promote_new_leader protocol)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral core: pre-spawn N threads; each runs join(), which under the pool synchronizer waits while a leader exists, claims the leader slot, releases the synchronizer and blocks in the demultiplexer on the shared handle set. When the wait returns an event, the leader re-acquires the synchronizer, clears the leader slot, signals one follower (promotion), releases it, deactivates the ready handle from the set, runs the handler itself as a processing thread, then reactivates the handle and loops back to join(). Keep the handle -> handler mapping in a demultiplexing table or registry, share one synchronizer among all followers, and make the promotion order an explicit decision (LIFO for cache affinity, priority order for real-time pools, FIFO or per-thread contexts for bound associations, and the native synchronizer's order only when simplicity outweighs cache behaviour). Pool sizing: N = C × U × (1 + W/S) where C=cores, U=target CPU utilisation, W=wait time, S=service time; for CPU-bound work use N = C + 1; for I/O-bound work a typical range is N × 5 to N × 50 depending on wait/compute ratio.
code_sketch:
join():                        # runs on every pool thread
  lock(pool)
  while leader != NONE: wait(followers_cv)   # follower
  leader = self(); unlock(pool)              # become leader
  events = demultiplex(handle_set)           # the leader's wait
  lock(pool)
  leader = NONE; signal(followers_cv)        # promote a follower
  unlock(pool)
  for e in events:
      deactivate(e.handle)                   # no double dispatch
      dispatch(handle_table[e.handle], e)    # process as ex-leader
      reactivate(e.handle)
pitfalls: Promotion and rejoin race with each other: every pool-state transition must happen under the pool synchronizer, and the synchronizer must never be held while waiting for events or running a handler.
Without the deactivate/reactivate step the newly promoted leader demultiplexes the same event a second time.
A processing thread cannot detect new events; nested waits must be designed as bound thread/handle associations with explicit hand-offs.
Skipping the deactivate step causes duplicate dispatch; skipping the reactivate step causes the event to never be noticed again.
Holding the pool lock across the demultiplexer wait serialises all followers and creates a thundering-herd on wakeup.
On NUMA systems, all threads accessing the same epoll fd rb-tree causes cache-line invalidation storms on the memory bus; consider sharding by handle-set.

Burst traffic can drain the pool entirely: if all N threads become processing threads simultaneously, no leader exists and incoming events sit in the kernel buffer until one handler returns - instrument this window.

Wrong move: hold the pool synchronizer while calling select()/poll() -> followers cannot wait or be promoted and wakeup contention serializes the pool -> instead release the synchronizer before demultiplexing and reacquire it only for role transitions.

Wrong move: run blocking database, file, or downstream-RPC work inside an unbound processing handler -> enough handlers can occupy every thread, leaving no leader and pushing latency into kernel buffers -> instead keep handlers non-blocking or hand blocking work to a separate executor or deliberately bound variant.

Wrong move: treat level-triggered readiness as one-shot without deactivation and rearm -> a promoted leader can dispatch the same readiness repeatedly, or a forgotten rearm can lose future events -> instead deactivate before dispatch and explicitly rearm after handling, or use an appropriate edge/one-shot mode.
sources: Schmidt, O'Ryan, Pyarali, Kircher & Buschmann, 'Leader/Followers: A Design Pattern for Efficient Multi-threaded Event Demultiplexing and Dispatching', PLoP 2000 / POSA2.
